title: ops-led-field-playbook-hyperscaler-tradeoffs
content:
Executive summary:

This playbook is written for field reps and solutions engineers who are engaging ops-first, platform, and SRE buyers when hyperscaler-managed AI endpoints (AWS SageMaker/Bedrock, GCP Vertex AI, Azure OpenAI Managed Endpoints) are on the short list. Goal: provide crisp, operationally-focused rebuttals and win themes that shift the buying decision toward Redwood Inference by highlighting predictable economics, deployment controls, and production resilience.

TL;DR win themes (one-liners for decks and emails):
- Predictable unit economics: Reserved capacity and smart batching reduce per-token cost and cost surprises vs variable hyperscaler managed pricing.
- Operational control without reinventing infra: Dedicated/private options give platform teams network policy, KMS, and observability comparable to internal endpoints but with less ops burden.
- Graceful degradation and multi-tier routing: Keep customer-facing experiences live by routing across model variants, regions, and capacity tiers — managed endpoints typically offer blunt fallbacks.
- Developer ergonomics for production: The same API, local testing, and rollout primitives (canaries, A/B, auto-fallback) that engineers expect from internal platforms, but maintained for you.

Target buyer personas and signals to watch for:
- Platform / ML Platform Lead (ops-focused): asks about fleet management, cost variability, and SLAs. Signals: questions about telemetry export, RBAC, KMS, and VPC peering.
- SRE / Infra Manager: cares about latency SLOs, failover behavior, and throttling behavior. Signals: mentions autoscaling limits, burst performance, and regional failover.
- Security/Compliance: demands audit logs, customer-managed keys, and private control plane. Signals: references to SOC2, FedRAMP, air-gap requirements.
- ML Engineer / Applied ML: wants correct model semantics across versions and stable KV cache behavior. Signals: test-suite regressions, model pinning requests, eval drift concerns.

Hyperscaler-managed endpoint plays — what they’ll say and how to rebut them:
1) Hyperscaler: “One bill, one vendor — easiest path.”
  - Rebuttal: Simplicity for invoices hides operational risk. When you need predictable unit economics (forecasting, reserved capacity), their bursty pricing and per-request addons create cost variability. Use Redwood’s reserved pools + batching examples to show smoothing of spend. Offer a short model: show naive hyperscaler per-token cost vs Redwood reserved baseline for 100M tokens/month.
2) Hyperscaler: “We already manage infra; trust our scaling.”
  - Rebuttal: Managed autoscaling is generic. Platform teams want fine-grained control (policy-driven routing, capacity tiers, warm pools, pre-warmed KV caches). Redwood exposes those controls with ops-grade APIs and SLO-targeted fallbacks.
3) Hyperscaler: “Security: our IAM + VPC + private endpoints are enterprise-ready.”
  - Rebuttal: True, but customers need control-plane separation, customer-managed KMS/HSM, and auditability that’s operationally testable. Redwood Private provides a private control plane option and on-prem packaging for highly regulated environments.
4) Hyperscaler: “Lowest latency in-region.”
  - Rebuttal: Latency claims are workload-dependent (sequence length, KV-cache hit rate, batching). We own kernel selection and runtime optimizations; for typical e-commerce/chat workloads Redwood often outperforms under predictable tail latency SLAs thanks to continuous batching and smarter pre-warming. Share microbenchmark graphs from internal repo (linked_artifacts).

Proof points and data to arm the field (short snippets for slides/emails):
- Cost smoothing: case study snippet — Est. 32% reduction in per-token cost using Redwood reserved pools + batching on mid-sized conversational workload vs hyperscaler managed endpoint (customer pseudonym: RetailCo).
- Failure blast radius: Using multi-tier routing reduced production incidents impacting user-facing latency by 63% in a recent internal canary test.
- Deployment friction: Customer security review time reduced from 8 weeks to 3 weeks when using Redwood Private (with documented network and KMS playbook).
- Developer experience: Same API for hosted/dedicated/private reduced integration effort by 2–3 sprints for an internal platform team (DevTime metric from SolutionsEng pilot).

Operational objections and rebuttals (quick):
- "We don’t want another vendor to manage." — Offer dedicated capacity + playbook for handover; emphasize runbooks, runbook drills, and joint runbooks during first 90 days.
- "We need on-prem/air-gapped." — Redwood Private is explicitly designed for this; reference the on-prem packaging checklist and audit artifacts.
- "We rely on existing cloud IAM/key rotations." — We integrate with customer KMS/HSM and support automated key rotation hooks; provide architecture diagram in repo.

Battle-tested playbook: how to run a 30–60–90 engagement with an ops-first buyer
- Discovery (0–2 weeks): map SLOs, current cost variability, telemetry endpoints (Prometheus/Datadog), compliance gates. Ask for token-volume histograms and p95/p99 latency targets.
- Pilot (2–6 weeks): small production slice behind canary routing. Provision a reserved pool sized for expected peak qps with a fallback to lower-cost hosted variant. Deliver dashboard visibility for token-level cost and per-request traces.
- Scale & handoff (6–12 weeks): configure autoscaling policies, policy documentation for failover, and run a staged rollout. Provide a 90-day optimization plan with quantized batching/quantization recommendations.

Sales motions and collateral required (quick checklist):
- One-page ops cheat sheet: Reserved Capacity math & example billing comparison (create for each buyer size).
- Runbook template: On-call handover + incident playbook for model regressions.
- Pilot config templates: Terraform snippets, RBAC examples, KMS integration guide.
- Benchmark artifacts: latency and cost microbench reports for small/medium/large workloads.

Sample field email (subject + 2–3 lines):
Subject: Low-friction pilot to stabilize inference costs and SLOs
Hi <name>,
We’ve helped platform teams reduce token cost volatility and close production gaps by combining reserved GPU pools with workload-aware batching. Can we run a 3-week pilot to show a live cost and latency comparison with your current managed endpoint? We’ll deliver dashboards and an ops-runbook you can keep.

Talk tracks for demos (30–90s snippets):
- For SRE: “We’ll show your p95/p99 under real traffic with reserved capacity, and then flip the fallback to hosted variants to prove graceful degradation — no finger-pointing during incidents.”
- For Platform Lead: “We’re not asking you to rip out your infra — Redwood sits alongside and gives you predictable unit economics, developer-friendly APIs, and control-plane isolation for security audits.”
- For Security: “Here’s the KMS workflow and audit trail; you keep your keys and we provide immutable logs and exportable evidence.”

Competitive landmines (things to avoid or prepare for):
- Avoid getting drawn into a pure feature checklist comparison with hyperscalers (they will always have a longer laundry list). Instead, focus on operational outcomes (cost predictability, SLO attainment, production resilience).
- Don’t promise deep feature parity in edge cases — commit to the migration plan and measurable outcomes for the pilot.

Open asks for GTM and product (what we need from teams):
- Marketing: Ops cheat-sheet template + two pager with reserved capacity math and an industry-agnostic case study.
- Product: Pilot-friendly default config for reserved pools + quick toggle for canary routing. Instrument a short telemetry export endpoint for pilot customers.
- Solutions Eng: Pre-written Terraform snippets and a runbook for first 90 days.

Next steps (field-owner checklist):
- Tailor the one-page ops cheat sheet to prospect size and attach to pilot proposal.
- Book a 45-min technical discovery with SRE + Platform Lead. Bring the runbook and cost-scenario model.
- After discovery, spin up a pilot environment with reserved pool + canary and schedule a 2-week demo showing cost/latency dashboards.

Author notes: this is intentionally ops-focused and deliberately avoids product feature laundry lists. Keep the messaging outcome-driven — reduce cost variance, increase predictability, and minimize incident blast radius.
